trajectory_summary: This is a fast, functional call: legitimacy established immediately, verify items covered in under four minutes, and a specific day/time booked that fits the customer's unusual night-shift schedule. The read is mixed rather than clean, though, because a credit-threshold number drifts from schema, a sub-threshold credit score is qualified past on the spouse's number without any stated resolution path, and the customer's core cost anxiety resurfaces unresolved in the closing seconds.

observed_outcome.quote: So that's tomorrow, the nineteenth, at 03:30PM.

That'd work.'), and the rep frames it as someone stopping by, indicating an in-person specialist visit. The wife/co-owner is identified on the title but never explicitly confirmed as attending the appointment.

bill_anchor_audit.reasoning: The rep acknowledges the range ('Dang. Yeah. That's quite the range there.') and lets the customer explain it's a new home on mostly gas heat, but never turns the number — or the flagged likely-summer increase — into a stated reason to act; the bill is captured and filed, not flipped.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep directly answers the stated cost-fear with the no-out-of-pocket / bill-swap framing immediately after it's raised, which is a genuine use of the customer's stated reason — though it is not reinforced again when the same fear resurfaces at 05:19.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: credit qualification on stated (not pulled) score, plus threshold drift
primary_coaching_focus.quote: I think I have, like, a six zero four. My wife has a higher one. She's close to 700,
primary_coaching_focus.why: This call gives management two concrete, stackable data points to bring to Kenny: the rep stated 650 instead of the schema's 670, and then qualified a customer whose own stated score (604) clears neither number by routing through the co-owner's score. Individually coachable, but more valuable as floor-wide evidence for resolving the open stated-vs-pulled credit policy question.

key_moments.quote: the requirements to qualify are to have a form of taxable income and a credit score of six fifty or higher.
key_moments.stewart_read: Rep states the credit threshold as 650, matching the exact drift pattern already documented in the schema from a prior call (SESSION18_fcbf33c1 also said 650 against a canonical 670). This is a repeatable floor-wide drift, not a one-off rep error.

key_moments.quote: I think I have, like, a six zero four. My wife has a higher one. She's close to 700,
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer's stated credit (604) sits below both the schema's 670 and the rep's stated 650, yet the rep qualifies the household through the co-owner spouse's higher stated score without pausing on Robert's own number. This is a live instance of the schema's unresolved policy question: should a setter DQ or pass through on stated (not pulled) credit, and whose score controls in a joint-title household?

key_moments.quote: Well, so it's been winter. We just bought the house, Two months ago,
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer hands the rep a live anchor — a brand-new home, currently gas-heavy, with an unknown summer electric load once AC kicks in ('with summertime, I don't know how high it'll be'). The rep acknowledges warmly but files it as small talk rather than reflecting it back as forward-pulling curiosity about how much the bill could grow.

key_moments.quote: Sounds good. Well, yeah, that's pretty much all the questions we have here for you.
key_moments.stewart_read: The rep closes out verify very quickly — the interest-in-solar answer (advertisement + cost fear) got one acknowledging line and no follow-up, and the bill range ($100-200, described by the customer himself as unreliable due to winter/gas heat) wasn't probed for the more telling summer figure. This is a verify-depth gap, not scope creep — the rep never over-explained product, he simply didn't deepen the two anchor questions the schema flags as highest-value (interest reason and bill).
